plan.title: Quantitative Multispecies eDNA
plan.outro: One qPCR anchor, thirteen species mapped.

beats.narration: A bottle of seawater holds DNA from dozens of fish,
but sequencing only tells you proportions, never how much.
That's the gap this project closes.
It's a reproducible research pipeline that joins two kinds of evidence:
qPCR, which measures the absolute amount of one reference species, hake,
and metabarcoding, which reads every species at once but only as shares.
Feed both into one joint statistical model,
and the shares turn into estimated DNA concentrations for every species.
From there, spatial smooths spread those estimates across the survey area,
so you get maps with uncertainty,
and finally every figure in the manuscript.
Reproducing it starts with one script.
You clone the repository, open the R project, and run the zero file.
It pulls the data archive from Zenodo,
fetches the raw reads from the sequence archive,
and stitches them into one combined file.
Then three notebooks run in order.
The first fits the joint model in Stan, alongside a mock community calibration that learns how each species amplifies.
The second fits the spatial smooths.
The third draws the figures.
And because each stage caches its outputs,
you can skip the expensive model fitting and jump straight to the maps.
The downloader even remembers what failed, so a broken run retries alone.
One known species, measured exactly, ends up anchoring the whole ocean's count.
